responses.strategic_rationale: The project targets the core tensions between resilience, sovereignty, and the economics of digital identity. It confronts supplier concentration risk by advocating platform-neutral access paths and credible fallback mechanisms, while balancing policy advocacy, procurement leverage, and standards pressure. The levers aim to de-risk a future state where Danish public services remain accessible even if Apple/Google platform signals shift or distribution terms change. Success hinges on credible demonstrations, regulatory engagement, and EU-aligned standards that collectively raise the cost of lock-in for incumbents while preserving public accountability and rapid, lawful progress.

levers.name: Platform-neutral fallback requirements in AltID procurement
levers.consequences: Shifting procurement toward platform-neutral fallback paths should increase resilience by reducing dependence on a single vendor baseline, while elevating governance requirements and pushing incumbents to demonstrate compliance. Downstream, procurement cycles may lengthen as standards are validated and enforcement processes are established, requiring stronger contract management and risk oversight.
options: Mandate platform-neutral fallback requirements in AltID procurement specs and require formal risk assessments of reliance on Apple and Google platform signals.
Adopt an open, standards-based fallback architecture using FIDO2/WebAuthn and OpenID Connect that can be verified independently of platform telemetry.
Create an open-source reference implementation and accompanying test plans to demonstrate secure fallback authentication across multiple vendors.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: procurement cycles may lengthen as standards are validated; gap: enforcement against incumbent resistance and pace of contract updates remain unaddressed.

levers.name: Demonstrator program to prove fallback feasibility
levers.consequences: A credible demonstrator program can de-risk the concept and build stakeholder buy-in, but it consumes limited funding and time that could otherwise support policy work or procurement planning. Downstream, success may raise expectations for rapid deployment that the project cannot meet.
options: Develop a mobile-oriented demonstrator on privacy-respecting Android with FIDO2/WebAuthn and OpenID Connect to validate a platform-neutral authentication path in isolation.
Create a browser-based fallback demonstrator using hardware tokens and WebAuthn to illustrate independence from mobile OS integrity signals.
Establish a cross-vendor interoperability lab to test end-to-end fallback access within a controlled identity-provider environment.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: demos stay in lab conditions and may not map to production integration; gap: insufficient demonstration of operator risk, procurement, and deployment pathways.

levers.name: Coalition-building for resilience framing and procurement leverage
levers.consequences: Building a broad coalition increases legitimacy and reduces policy-friction risk, but may slow decision-making if stakeholders disagree on messaging. Downstream, alignment challenges can arise when translating advocacy into binding procurement commitments.
options: Form formal partnerships with civil-society groups, privacy advocates, and researchers to push resilience framing and procurement-neutral language across policy briefs.
Engage Folketinget's digital policy committee early to secure oversight commitments and reduce friction at milestone reviews.
Coordinate with EU partners to align on AltID and wallet standards, creating a joint advocacy position that adds pressure to procurement decisions.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: coalition-building can slow decision-making and produce competing messaging; gap: lacking commitments from key policymakers to translate advocacy into binding procurement changes.

levers.name: Standards-driven alignment with NSIS/eIDAS and AltID
levers.consequences: Aligning standards strengthens interoperability and reduces platform lock-in, but external validation can slow procurement and create conflicts with domestic timeline needs. Downstream, gaps may appear in how audits are administered and how results influence vendor selection.
options: Push binding NSIS/eIDAS-aligned standards into AltID procurement to require cross-vendor interoperability tests and independent verification.
Sponsor EU-level interoperability studies to craft shared reference architectures for platform-neutral fallback pathways across member states.
Finance independent standards-compliance audits of fallback components and publish results to build credibility with public-sector buyers.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: external standards validation can slow procurement and reveal gaps; gap: domestic governance and enforcement mechanisms to implement NSIS/eIDAS-aligned tests are not specified.

levers.name: Alternative trust anchors governance for fallback ecosystem
levers.consequences: Establishing governance around a certified fallback path reduces single-point failure and enables multiple providers, but adds administrative complexity and potential fragmentation. Downstream, clear accountability requires funding and formal authorization channels.
options: Propose a governance model for a certified fallback path anchored in public-sector trust with independent oversight and clear accountability.
Define platform-agnostic trust anchors such as national PKI and open-source identity components that multiple vendors can adopt.
Pilot staged deployment with defined service levels and continuity commitments across several identity providers to stress-test resilience.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: governance complexity increases administration overhead; gap: clear authority, funding, and enforcement mechanisms for a shared fallback ecosystem are not defined.

levers.name: EU procurement harmonization and cross-border adoption dynamics
levers.consequences: Engaging EU-level standards and procurement norms can broaden legitimacy and reduce risk of national lock-in, but may complicate timelines and domestic decision autonomy. Downstream, alignment with EU expectations can demand additional coordination and resources.
options: Engage EU bodies to influence wallet standards and procurement guidelines toward platform neutrality and fallback readiness.
Coordinate with multiple member states to pilot a joint procurement model for fallback authentication solutions and shared evaluation criteria.
Publish position papers that shape European Digital Identity Wallet architecture while preserving national procurement prerogatives.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: EU alignment may extend timelines; gap: concrete domestic funding commitments and governance rights to act on EU guidance are unclear.

responses.strategic_rationale: Denmark's digital identity strategy faces a core tension between preserving service continuity and reducing dependence on a small number of foreign platform providers. The levers focus on platform-neutral fallback authentication, diversified procurement, EU interoperability, coalition-based legitimacy, standards-driven architecture, and resilience planning. Together they aim to shift procurement and standards toward supplier-agnostic paths while preserving oversight and user trust. The plan prioritizes governance, policy engagement, and credible demonstrations over immediate replacement of MitID, recognizing the inertia of incumbents and regulatory friction. By combining resilience framing with procurement leverage and technical demonstrations, the project seeks durable changes in AltID design language and vendor-ecosystem expectations, reducing single-vendor risk without sacrificing compliance and privacy.

levers.name: Platform-neutral certification pathway for fallback access
levers.consequences: Establishing the platform-neutral certification pathway increases resilience by reducing reliance on a single platform, enabling continuity during platform outages. It also adds integration and regulatory compliance overhead and requires ongoing governance to sustain cross-platform compatibility.
options: Establish a standards-aligned fallback authentication path using FIDO2/WebAuthn and OpenID Connect across certified devices, documenting interoperability outcomes with AltID.
Embed platform-neutral trust anchors into procurement language and contract clauses, ensuring supplier audits verify independence from Apple/Google signals.
Run a live, non-production pilot across municipal services to test continuity, user experience, and regulatory compliance for platform-neutral fallback access.
levers.review_lever: Adopting a platform-neutral fallback path improves resilience by reducing vendor lock-in, but the complexity and cost of cross-platform integration may erode early benefits unless regulatory support and funding timelines align; the three options leave interoperability milestones under-defined.

levers.name: Procurement reform to reduce supplier-concentration risk in AltID framework
levers.consequences: Shifting procurement to diversify suppliers reduces single-vendor risk and improves continuity. It also extends procurement cycles and increases administrative overhead, and may provoke political resistance from incumbents that slow progress.
options: Propose phased procurement criteria that separate device-entrained trust signals from identity verification, enabling alternative channel validations.
Advocate for procurement blocks that require vendor diversity, including at least two independent platform environments for essential services.
Develop a procurement playbook linking risk appetite to supplier concentration metrics, with transparent escalation paths for fallback-capable designs.
levers.review_lever: Shifting procurement to diversify suppliers reduces single-vendor risk and improves continuity. It also extends procurement cycles and raises administrative overhead, and may provoke political resistance from incumbents that slow progress.

levers.name: EU and NSIS-aligned interoperability advocacy for platform-agnostic identity
levers.consequences: Aligning with EU NSIS and interoperability agendas can unlock broader adoption, but may slow domestic timelines and require concessions on national policy priorities and budget timing.
options: Coordinate with EU working groups to publish Danish positions on platform-neutral wallets, portability, and continuity requirements.
Draft policy notes translating fallback authentication concepts into EU procurement criteria and technical standards for AltID.
Organize a cross-border proof-of-concept with adjacent privacy and security agencies to validate interoperability across ecosystems.
levers.review_lever: Aligning with EU NSIS and interoperability agendas can unlock broader adoption, but may dilute national policy priorities and delay immediate Danish procurement wins; the three options leave domestic sovereignty considerations and budget timing under-addressed.

levers.name: Coalition-building for platform-neutral access acceptance
levers.consequences: Building a broad coalition creates legitimacy and diverse insight, but it can slow decision-making and generate conflicting priorities; the three options fail to specify accountable governance structures and funding commitments within the coalition.
options: Establish a multi-stakeholder coalition with civil society, academia, and regional authorities to co-author resilience and continuity policy proposals.
Launch a formal public consultation and feedback loop to capture user concerns about fallback access and privacy implications.
Securing parliamentary hearings and committee briefings to elevate fallback-platform discussions within procurement reform agendas.
levers.review_lever: Building a broad coalition creates legitimacy and diverse insight, but it can slow decision-making and generate conflicting priorities, risking ambiguous accountability and funding commitments.

levers.name: Standards-driven architectural blueprint for AltID resilience
levers.consequences: Publishing a standards-driven blueprint clarifies components and interfaces, enabling procurement pressure for resilience, yet risks constraining iterative innovation and creating rigid adherence timelines that are hard to adjust as threat models evolve.
options: Publish a standards-compliant blueprint detailing minimal viable components for platform-neutral identity and resilient fallback channels.
Form an open-standards working group to align device trust signals, browser-based access, and wallet interoperability.
Commission independent security reviews of the fallback architecture to identify gaps in chain-of-trust and governance.
levers.review_lever: Publishing a standards-driven blueprint clarifies components and interfaces, enabling procurement pressure for resilience, yet risks constraining iterative innovation and creating rigid adherence timelines that are hard to adjust as threat models evolve.

levers.name: Public-sector continuity simulations and tabletop exercises
levers.consequences: Regular continuity exercises strengthen institutional muscle and reveal gaps early, but they consume budget and staff time that could be diverted to concrete pilots; the three options do not ensure immediate transition paths or formal decision rights from exercises.
options: Conduct regular continuity tabletop exercises across agencies to stress-test fallback authentication under outage scenarios.
Document decision gates and escalation procedures for platform compromise, ensuring clear lines of responsibility and fallback activation triggers.
Simulate supply-chain disruptions and simulate vendor failures to quantify impact on service continuity and regulatory reporting obligations.
levers.review_lever: Regular continuity exercises strengthen institutional muscle and reveal gaps early, but they consume budget and staff time that could be diverted to concrete pilots; the three options do not ensure immediate transition paths or formal decision rights from exercises.

responses.strategic_rationale: Denmark’s 2026–2029 digital identity strategy emphasizes resilience, continuity, and reduced dependency on a small set of foreign platform providers. The core tension lies in balancing rapid continuity of public services with the need for platform-neutral fallbacks, credible standards pressure, and governance that incentivizes diversified trust anchors without destabilizing current MitID operations. The following levers push beyond incremental improvements by reframing procurement, standards alignment, and coalition-building as strategic instruments to decouple trust from OS market power while maintaining public accountability and security. The levers collectively address procurement neutrality, EU interoperability, vendor diversification, evidence-based certification, hardware-rooted alternatives, and inclusive governance.

levers.name: Fallback authentication governance for AltID delivery
levers.consequences: Pulling this lever creates a formal requirement for platform-neutral fallback authentication in AltID procurement documents, shaping supplier selection toward resilience. Downstream, governance overhead increases and procurement timelines may lengthen, while clarity on continuity obligations improves risk management.
options: Institute a formal policy mandating platform-neutral fallback authentication pathways in AltID procurement documents and supplier criteria.
Create a cross-ministerial governance board to oversee fallback authentication readiness, with quarterly reviews and decision gates.
Develop a risk-adjusted budget line to fund pilot testing of fallback methods across multiple service domains.
levers.review_lever: Primary trade-off is slower procurement due to governance overhead, and the three options leave unaddressed concrete budgeting and measurable fallback effectiveness.

levers.name: Public-sector interoperability alignment with European Wallet standards
levers.consequences: Pulling this lever aligns Danish requirements with European Wallet interoperability guidelines, reducing cross-border authentication friction and enabling smoother portability for public services. Downstream, governance overhead rises to track EU spec updates, and timelines may be affected if EU roadmaps shift or diverge from national needs.
options: Engage EU-level working groups to map Danish requirements to European Digital Identity Wallet interoperability guidelines and gaps.
Publish a policy brief detailing how Denmark will implement portability and cross-border authentication using European Wallet standards.
Pilot a cross-border test with a trusted Danish identity partner to demonstrate compliance with NSIS and eIDAS2 interoperability rules.
levers.review_lever: Primary trade-off is governance overhead and potential delay to EU-aligned timelines; the options do not specify a concrete plan for budget or regulatory alignment.

levers.name: Diversified procurement pilots with non-Apple/Google partners
levers.consequences: Reducing dependence on Apple/Google by testing multiple platform implementations and a hardware-backed backup path, the lever broadens the solution space. Downstream, integration complexity increases across vendors, contracting risk grows, and initial pilot costs may be higher before standardization.
options: Launch an early-stage pilot contracting with open OS or vendor-agnostic security stack providers to test fallback efficacy.
Solicit a multi-vendor bidding process featuring at least three independent platform implementations and a hardware-token backup path.
Establish a short-cycle procurement sandbox to compare platform-neutral candidates against incumbent MitID dependencies in practice.
levers.review_lever: Primary trade-off is increased coordination burden and higher vendor-management overhead; the options leave unaddressed how to scale beyond pilots within budget.

levers.name: Certified evidence program for platform-neutral access
levers.consequences: Establishing a certified evidence program creates independent validation of fallback approaches and NSIS-aligned pathways, boosting credibility with authorities and partners. Downstream, certification activities require budget and scheduling, potentially delaying milestones and narrowing experimentation tempo.
options: Commission an independent security review of proposed fallback implementations with publicly auditable criteria and transparency.
Create a certification path for fallback access that aligns with NSIS requirements and uses open test vectors.
Publish quarterly demonstration reports detailing security postures, interoperability tests, and remediation plans for fallback pathways.
levers.review_lever: Primary trade-off is certification bottlenecks slowing validation; the options do not specify funding envelopes or performance targets for reviews.

levers.name: Independent hardware-rooted trust anchor exploration
levers.consequences: Pursuing hardware-rooted trust anchors offers a tangible, platform-neutral foundation for identity signaling independent of OS ecosystems. Downstream, hardware supply constraints and user friction risks complicate rollout, with added integration and security-review requirements.
options: Commission a white-paper and small-scale prototype exploring hardware-based attestation as an alternative trust anchor for the fallback path.
Host a standards workshop with hardware-security labs to evaluate practical constraints and interoperability with existing AltID flows.
Prototype a tamper-evident device layer to isolate identity signaling from mobile OS during fallback tests.
levers.review_lever: Primary trade-off is hardware supply risk and user friction; the options leave unaddressed how to achieve scale and ensure standardization across devices.

levers.name: Distributed stakeholder co-design for resilient identity access
levers.consequences: Co-design with civil society and procurement officials builds legitimacy and aligns resilience expectations across stakeholders. Downstream, consensus-building slows decision cycles and can cause scope drift unless clear governance and decision gates are established.
options: Coordinate a structured co-design forum including civil society, privacy advocates, and procurement officials to shape requirements.
Run a scenario-planning exercise focused on outage response, including governance, communications, and service level expectations.
Develop a public-facing road-map detailing milestones, decision gates, and accountability for platform-neutral access work progress.
levers.review_lever: Primary trade-off is time-to-decision and potential scope creep; the options lack explicit decision gates or accountability mechanisms.

system_prompt:
You are an expert strategic analyst. Generate solution space parameters following these directives:

1. **Output Requirements**
   - You must generate 5 to 7 levers per response.
   - Each lever's `options` field must contain exactly 3 qualitative strategic choices as plain strings.

2. **Lever Quality Standards**
   - Consequences: describe the direct effect of pulling this lever, then at least one downstream implication or trade-off. Be concise and grounded — only cite specific numbers if the project context provides evidence for them. Do not fabricate percentages or cost estimates. Target length: 2–4 sentences.
   - Options MUST:
     • Represent genuinely distinct strategic pathways (not just labels)
     • Include at least one unconventional or non-obvious approach
     • NO prefixes (e.g., "Option A:", "Choice 1:")

3. **Strategic Framing**
   - Name each lever using language drawn directly from the project's own domain — avoid formulaic patterns or repeated prefixes
   - Frame options as complete strategic approaches
   - Ensure levers challenge core project assumptions

4. **Validation Protocols**
   - For `review_lever`:
     A short critical review — identify the primary trade-off this lever introduces, then state the specific gap the three options leave unaddressed.
     Examples:
     - "Switching from seasonal contract labor to year-round employees stabilizes harvest quality, but the idle-wage burden during the 5-month off-season adds a fixed cost that erases the per-unit savings unless utilization reaches year-round levels."
     - "Each additional clinical site requires its own IRB approval, site-initiation visit, and staff credentialing — a sequential overhead that compounds rather than parallelizes, so doubling site count does not halve enrollment time."
     - "Pooling catastrophe risk across three coastal regions reduces expected annual loss on paper, but a single regional hurricane season can correlate all three simultaneously, turning the diversification assumption into a concentration risk at the worst possible moment."
     Do not use square brackets or placeholder text.

5. **Prohibitions**
   - NO prefixes/labels in options (e.g., "Option A:", "Choice 1:")
   - NO generic option labels (e.g., "Optimize X", "Tolerate Y")
   - NO placeholder consequences or bracket-wrapped templates
   - NO fabricated statistics or percentages without evidence from the project context
   - NO marketing language (e.g., "game-changing", "cutting-edge", "revolutionary")

6. **Length Limits**
   - Keep each `review_lever` to one sentence (20–40 words). State the trade-off and the gap concisely.
   - Each option should be a concrete, actionable approach (at least 15 words with an action verb) — not a short label or vague aspiration

Plan:
Denmark's national digital identity infrastructure currently depends in practice on Apple iOS and Google Android for broad citizen access to essential services such as banking, tax filing, healthcare portals, and public administration. This dependency is not limited to app-store distribution. MitID's anti-fraud and app-integrity model relies on platform-controlled signals concerning approved installation channels and device integrity, which means that critical parts of the trust model for Danish digital identity are mediated by two foreign commercial platform providers. Even where direct observation of specific authentication events is not publicly documented, the current setup leaves Danish digital identity structurally dependent on platform vendors that control app availability, device trust signals, and surrounding telemetry environments. This creates not only a digital-sovereignty problem, but also a resilience and contingency problem: essential public access depends on a narrow supplier base and lacks a clearly platform-neutral fallback path.

This matters because Denmark's public-sector digital strategy for 2026–2029 explicitly calls for reduced dependence on a small number of large foreign technology suppliers and for stronger digital sovereignty. The issue should therefore not be framed only as privacy or ideology, but as a concrete public-sector risk involving supplier concentration, reduced strategic autonomy, continuity-of-service exposure, and the absence of a robust fallback authentication path if platform policies, integrity APIs, distribution terms, or geopolitical conditions change.

This project does not attempt to build and certify a production-ready replacement for MitID within the current trust framework. That would be unrealistic. The MitID ecosystem is conservative, certification-heavy, and tightly coupled to Apple/Google platform integrity signals. Instead, the project's objective is to establish the technical, regulatory, and political basis for formal platform-neutral access requirements and a certified fallback authentication path for Danish digital identity. The primary intervention point is not retrofitting MitID itself, but influencing AltID — Denmark's staged eIDAS2 wallet rollout — together with related procurement, standards, and continuity-planning decisions before the next identity stack hardens the same dependencies.

The project is structured in three phases over 24 months with a total budget of 10.5 million DKK, gated across phases (3.0 million for phase one, 4.0 million for phase two, 3.5 million for phase three). The higher budget reflects the need for credible technical work, policy engagement, external review, institutional overhead, and contingency capacity. Do not assume that 8 million DKK is sufficient for the same scope.

Phase one (months 1–8) is a feasibility, risk, and coalition-building phase. The technical work maps the relevant MitID dependency surface, especially platform integrity assumptions, app-distribution constraints, and the architectural conditions required for a platform-neutral or fallback trust model under eIDAS and NSIS at level "Substantial" or higher. The policy work reframes the issue in terms of resilience, continuity of service, procurement neutrality, and supplier concentration risk, while also addressing privacy and democratic accountability. In parallel, the advocacy work builds a coalition spanning civil-society organisations, privacy advocates, academic researchers, security experts, contingency-planning stakeholders, and sympathetic members of Folketinget's digital policy committee. The deliverables are: (1) a published feasibility and risk report, (2) a formal policy proposal to Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, (3) a fallback-authentication concept note oriented toward AltID and future procurement requirements, and (4) a permit/approval and stakeholder matrix with lead times, decision gates, and identified blockers. Phase one funding is unconditional.

Phase two (months 9–16) develops non-production technical demonstrators. These are not certified MitID clients and do not attempt production integration with live MitID systems. The main demonstrator authenticates against a simulated Danish public-sector identity-provider environment using open standards such as FIDO2/WebAuthn and OpenID Connect on GrapheneOS or one comparable privacy-respecting Android-compatible platform. A secondary demonstrator explores a browser-based or hardware-token-based fallback authentication path that reduces dependence on the mobile OS duopoly altogether. The goal is not to prove immediate deployability, but to produce credible technical evidence that secure, standards-based, fallback-capable access models are feasible without exclusive reliance on Apple or Google as trust anchors. Keep the demonstrator scope lean and defensible; do not expand into feature-rich product development. Phase two funding is conditional on phase one producing a published feasibility report, at least one formal institutional engagement with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, the MitID operator, or a related public-sector stakeholder, and a documented financing plan covering the remainder of the project.

Phase three (months 17–24) focuses on procurement, standards, and continuity intervention around AltID and related digital identity planning. Using the feasibility report, demonstrators, and coalition built in earlier phases, the project seeks inclusion of requirements stating that Danish digital identity systems should not depend exclusively on Apple or Google app stores, platform integrity APIs, or proprietary push-notification infrastructure, and should include a platform-neutral or otherwise certified fallback access path for critical public authentication. The project also engages with relevant EU bodies and technical working groups connected to the European Digital Identity Wallet framework, with the aim of aligning Danish advocacy with broader European requirements on interoperability, portability, resilience, and reduced platform lock-in. The project's role is not to dictate architecture directly, but to create technical evidence, procurement language, and standards pressure that make supplier-neutral and fallback-capable design harder to exclude. If formal traction with AltID is weak by month 16, phase three should de-scope toward publication, coalition consolidation, and EU-facing standards input rather than pretending Danish procurement influence has been secured.

The project team should include a lead researcher in mobile security and authentication protocols, a regulatory and compliance specialist familiar with Danish and EU digital identity frameworks (including eIDAS and NSIS), a policy and public-affairs coordinator experienced in Danish digital governance and procurement processes, a technical lead for the demonstrator work, and at least one additional engineer or contractor covering web authentication, hardware-token workflows, or Linux/GrapheneOS-related implementation. The technical staffing should avoid dependence on a single specialist. Assume the project's primary physical base is in Copenhagen, Denmark, at a Danish university, independent research institution, or security-qualified R&D facility providing access-controlled workspace appropriate for security-sensitive digital identity research, development, and stakeholder meetings. Budget for institutional overhead, external security review, and limited legal/procurement support explicitly rather than treating them as absorbed costs.

Success criteria: by month 24, the project has produced a published feasibility and risk report on platform-neutral and fallback-capable Danish digital identity; delivered two working non-production demonstrators (one mobile-oriented, one browser-based or hardware-token-based fallback); secured a formal written response from Digitaliseringsstyrelsen or another relevant authority to the project's proposal; and achieved inclusion of platform-neutrality, fallback access, continuity, resilience, or supplier-concentration language in at least one official AltID-related design, policy, consultation, or procurement document. A stretch goal is that the project's EU-level engagement contributes to language in relevant European Digital Identity Wallet materials that supports platform-neutral access or certified fallback mechanisms. Do not use consumer adoption rates as a primary KPI for this project, because it is not shipping a production identity product.

Pick a realistic scenario that accounts for institutional inertia, regulatory friction, incumbent resistance, financing uncertainty, and the likelihood that convenience arguments will be used against platform-neutral alternatives. Do not assume constructive cooperation from existing operators. The primary lever is not technical disruption for its own sake, but the combination of resilience framing, procurement intervention, standards pressure, and credible technical demonstration.
